items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “Advertising that gives factual information about a product’s features, price or benefits”?
items.answer: Informational advertising
items.markingKey: Informational advertising: advertising that gives factual information about a product’s features, price or benefits. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between informational and transformational advertising.
items.answer: Informational advertising presents facts (features, price, performance) to persuade rationally; transformational advertising associates the product with feelings, images or lifestyles to change how using it feels.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of television as an advertising medium.
items.answer: Advantage: reaches a large audience with sound and moving images, attracting attention. Disadvantage: expensive and viewers may skip or ignore adverts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A sports brand in Dhaka is launching new running shoes aimed at teenagers and asks Tomás to plan the advertising. Suggest one type of advertising Tomás could use and explain why.
items.answer: Transformational advertising showing teenagers enjoying running with friends, because teenagers are influenced by lifestyle and social image; or celebrity endorsement by a young athlete.
items.markingKey: 1 mark type; 1 mark justification [2]

items.stem: “The AIDA model of advertising has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including practicality in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (practicality): Each stage can be measured (for example attention by eye tracking, action by sales). Strength (usefulness): It gives advertisers a simple checklist for designing adverts that lead to purchase. Weakness (reductionism): It assumes a fixed sequence of stages, but consumers may buy on impulse or without interest. Weakness (supporting evidence): There is little experimental evidence that consumers pass through the stages in order. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Explain the elaboration likelihood model of persuasion.
items.answer: When motivation and ability to think about a message are high, people use the central route and are persuaded by strong arguments, producing lasting attitudes; when they are low, people use the peripheral route and are persuaded by cues such as attractive sources, producing temporary attitudes.

items.stem: Evaluate the elaboration likelihood model, including a discussion of usefulness.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Advertisers can match the type of advert to the involvement of the target audience. Strength (supporting evidence): Petty et al. (1983) showed involvement changed whether arguments or celebrities mattered, as predicted. Weakness (explanatory power): It is hard to know in advance which route a consumer will use, so predictions are difficult. Weakness (ecological validity): Much research used students rating mock adverts in a laboratory. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Discuss whether the elaboration likelihood model explains how advertising persuades consumers.
items.answer: Arguments for: High-involvement consumers are persuaded by strong arguments (central route); low-involvement consumers by cues such as celebrities (peripheral route) (Petty et al., 1983). Arguments against: The model does not explain why involvement varies. Emotional advertising can work in both routes. Much evidence comes from laboratory studies with students. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Explain why young children may be particularly vulnerable to advertising.
items.answer: Young children cannot reliably distinguish adverts from programmes or understand persuasive intent, so they accept advertising claims uncritically and develop strong brand preferences.

items.stem: Describe the findings of Fischer et al. (1991).
items.answer: Children aged 3–6 matched logos to products; recognition increased with age, and 91% of 6-year-olds matched Joe Camel with cigarettes, as well as they matched Mickey Mouse with the Disney Channel.

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Fischer et al.’s (1991) study of brand logo recognition by young children. Include at least one point about validity.
items.answer: Strength (standardisation): All children did the same matching task with the same logo cards and game board. Strength (usefulness): The findings informed campaigns to end cartoon characters in tobacco advertising. Weakness (generalisability): Children came from preschools in one area of the USA, so findings may not apply elsewhere. Weakness (validity): Matching a logo to a product shows recognition, not that children like the product or will use it. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that advertising to children should be banned? In your answer, you may refer to children and psychology, ethics and usefulness.
items.answer: Arguments for: Young children cannot recognise persuasive intent and are highly brand-aware (Fischer et al., 1991: 91% of 6-year-olds recognised Joe Camel). Advertising of unhealthy food is linked to children’s preferences. Arguments against: Parents can teach media literacy and children learn to recognise advertising as they grow older. Advertising funds children’s programmes and can promote healthy products. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.answer: (a) IV: whether the advert used strong arguments or a celebrity endorser. DV: attitude to the product on a 1–20 rating scale. (b) Strong arguments: 4; celebrity endorser: 9. (e) Repeated measures removes participant variables because the same people do both conditions, but order effects (practice or fatigue) and demand characteristics become more likely; counterbalancing would be needed.

(a) Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study. (b) Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place.
items.answer: (a) IV: whether the advert used strong arguments or a celebrity endorser. DV: attitude to the product on a 1–20 rating scale. (b) Strong arguments: 15.2; celebrity endorser: 10.7.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2] (b) Strong arguments: 91 ÷ 6 = 15.2; celebrity endorser: 64 ÷ 6 = 10.7. 1 mark for each correct mean [2]

items.stem: ‘The elaboration likelihood model explains how advertising persuades consumers.’ To what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Arguments for: High-involvement consumers are persuaded by strong arguments (central route); low-involvement consumers by cues such as celebrities (peripheral route) (Petty et al., 1983). Arguments against: The model does not explain why involvement varies. Emotional advertising can work in both routes. Much evidence comes from laboratory studies with students. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “Using a famous person to promote a product”?
items.answer: Celebrity endorsement
items.markingKey: Celebrity endorsement: using a famous person to promote a product. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “Celebrity endorsement can increase attention to an advert.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of television as an advertising medium.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Familiar faces attract attention and may transfer positive feelings. (b) Advantage: reaches a large audience with sound and moving images, attracting attention. Disadvantage: expensive and viewers may skip or ignore adverts.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: With reference to the AIDA model of advertising, explain one weakness relating to supporting evidence.
items.answer: There is little experimental evidence that consumers pass through the stages in order.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to supporting evidence; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Kwame showed 7 adults in Accra an advert for a new phone with strong arguments and 7 adults an advert with a famous celebrity and weak arguments. All were told they would soon choose a phone (high involvement). Attitude to the phone (1–20) was measured. Table: Attitude rating (1–20) — Strong arguments: 11, 12, 19, 14, 17, 16, 16. Celebrity endorser: 9, 13, 12, 13, 11, 9, 12. The standard deviation for the strong arguments condition was 2.83 and for the celebrity endorser condition was 1.70. Explain what these values show.
items.answer: The strong arguments condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2]

items.stem: A sports brand in Istanbul is launching new running shoes aimed at teenagers and asks Daniel to plan the advertising. (a) Suggest one type of advertising Daniel could use and explain why. (b) Explain how the AIDA model could guide the campaign.
items.answer: (a) Transformational advertising showing teenagers enjoying running with friends, because teenagers are influenced by lifestyle and social image; or celebrity endorsement by a young athlete. (b) Grab Attention with an eye-catching video, build Interest with features, create Desire with images of success, and prompt Action with a discount code.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark type; 1 mark justification [2] (b) 1 mark stages applied; 1 mark example [2]

items.stem: Design an observation to investigate how often adverts aimed at children are shown during children’s programmes. Your plan must include: behavioural categories, how inter-rater reliability will be checked and the sampling technique.
items.answer: Method: an observation. Structured observation with operationalised behavioural categories and time sampling; two observers to check inter-rater reliability; overt or covert as appropriate. Variables: behaviour: adverts shown; categories: food, toys, games, other. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Cairo, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “Persuasion through superficial cues such as attractiveness or celebrity, used when involvement is low”?
items.answer: Peripheral route
items.markingKey: Peripheral route: persuasion through superficial cues such as attractiveness or celebrity, used when involvement is low. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “Distraction can reduce a person’s ability to process arguments centrally.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Describe the findings of Petty, Cacioppo and Schumann (1983).
items.answer: (a) Correct. Ability to elaborate is reduced, so peripheral cues matter more. (b) High-involvement participants’ attitudes to a razor depended mainly on argument strength; low-involvement participants’ attitudes depended more on whether the endorsers were celebrities.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark high involvement; 1 mark low involvement [2]

items.stem: Outline one weakness of the elaboration likelihood model that relates to ecological validity.
items.answer: Much research used students rating mock adverts in a laboratory.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to ecological validity; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Ethan showed 7 adults in Toronto an advert for a new phone with strong arguments and 7 adults an advert with a famous celebrity and weak arguments. All were told they would soon choose a phone (high involvement). Attitude to the phone (1–20) was measured. Table: Attitude rating (1–20) — Strong arguments: 18, 15, 16, 14, 19, 13, 18. Celebrity endorser: 10, 11, 9, 10, 13, 11, 12. The participants were people who were in the college canteen at lunchtime when Ethan was collecting data. Identify the sampling technique used and explain one weakness of it.
items.answer: Opportunity sampling. Weakness: only people present at that place and time could be chosen, so the sample may be biased and not representative of the target population.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sampling technique; 1 mark: weakness explained [2]

items.stem: Freya is marketing two products in Jakarta: an expensive electric car and a cheap chocolate bar. Explain why attitudes formed through the central route are more useful to the car company.
items.answer: They are longer lasting and resistant to competitors’ messages, so buyers are more likely to stay committed until purchase.
items.markingKey: 1 mark durable; 1 mark benefit [2]

items.stem: Ines wants to find out whether children can tell the difference between adverts and programmes. Design a laboratory experiment to investigate this. Your plan must include: ethical issues, the sampling technique, the type of data collected and how the dependent variable will be measured.
items.answer: Method: a laboratory experiment. Manipulate the IV in a controlled room; standardised procedure and instructions; measure the DV objectively. Variables: IV: age of child; DV: number of adverts correctly identified. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Seoul, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.

items.stem: Define the term ‘persuasive intent’.
items.answer: The aim of an advert to make people want to buy something.
items.markingKey: Persuasive intent: the aim of an advert to make people want to buy something. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Outline one strength of Fischer et al.’s (1991) study of brand logo recognition by young children that relates to standardisation.
items.answer: All children did the same matching task with the same logo cards and game board.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to standardisation; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Explain one weakness of Fischer et al.’s (1991) study of brand logo recognition by young children in terms of validity.
items.answer: Matching a logo to a product shows recognition, not that children like the product or will use it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to validity; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Children of different ages in Lima were asked to match brand logos to products. The table shows correct and incorrect matches. 5-year-olds: correct 50, incorrect 12; 6-year-olds: correct 52, incorrect 4; 4-year-olds: correct 26, incorrect 21; 3-year-olds: correct 27, incorrect 34. (a) Calculate the percentage of matches for 4-year-olds that were “correct”. Give your answer to one decimal place. (b) Calculate the overall percentage of matches in the table that were “correct”.
items.markingKey: (a) 26 ÷ (26 + 21) × 100 = 26 ÷ 47 × 100 = 55.3%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) Total “correct” = 155; total = 226; 155 ÷ 226 × 100 = 68.6%. 1 mark totals; 1 mark answer [2]
